KEY MESSAGE 1...Dry and cool tonight. Heat and humidity begin 
to build for Wednesday. 

High pressure continues to dominate through Wednesday; however,
it will begin to weaken and move offshore tonight/early 
Wednesday. This will lead to winds turning more 
south/southwesterly... advecting higher temps and dewpoints into
southern New England into Wednesday. Given relatively clear 
skies and calm winds tonight, expecting another round of 
radiational cooling, although perhaps not as strong as last 
night. Overnight temps should drop into the upper 40s/low 50s 
tonight. Southwesterly flow Wednesday should begin to surge 
dewpoints back into the low 60s, and with temperatures climbing 
into the upper 70s or near 80, humidity will be on the rise 
leading to a muggy, sticky feeling.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Shower chances Thursday evening into Friday 
morning, followed by drier conditions Friday.

Mainly dry for Thursday; however, a northern-stream shortwave 
trough arrives late in the day and exits early Friday, bringing 
another round of showers to southern New England. Clouds are on 
the increase Thursday morning as higher moisture is pumped into 
the region. PWAT values are roughly 2 inches, which is near the 
maximum of climatology based on sounding climatology at Chatham.

Where confidence is lacking is with the forcing. The 15/12z NAM
12km and, to some extent, the 3km (though model guidance 
doesn't extend beyond 00z Friday) show robust forcing near the 
NYC metro. Meanwhile, farther northeast, there is less-than-
ideal forcing over southern New England. The ECMWF favors 
central New England for the better forcing, while the GFS and 
Canadian have very minimal forcing across central New England. 
Another limiting factor is the presence of dry air aloft in the 
mid-levels.

That being said, a subtle shift in the guidance to the 
northeast needs to be monitored, given the impressive swath of 
2-4", locally 5 inches, of rain this past Sunday. We'd like more
confidence in this part of the forecast given it is only a few 
days out, though when you have weakly forced environments, it 
can be difficult to pinpoint the exact details.

Current thinking favors the forcing across central New England,
as there has been continuity from run to run over the past 24 
hours and across multiple models. Went with a blend for the QPF 
forecast between our current forecast, NBM, and WPC. QPF is 
generally a few hundredths of an inch along the southern coast 
and perhaps a tenth of an inch along our northern borders with 
VT/NH. That said, I wouldn't fully discredit the NAM just yet. 
Something to monitor. Stay tuned for updates!

KEY MESSAGE 3...Next chance for rain returns Sunday, though 
confidence in exact timing remains low at this time.

A transient high pressure system moving out of the southern 
Canadian Prairies brings a dry stretch of weather Friday and 
Saturday. Seasonably mild temperatures are expected Friday, with
highs in the middle 70s and elevated dew points initially in 
the lower 60s, though those fall into the 50s by Friday 
afternoon. Then a shift to more fall-like conditions on 
Saturday, with highs in the middle to upper 60s and crisp air as
dew points fall into the 40s to lower 50s.

The weekend looks split, with rain returning Sunday. It's 
possible the early hours of the day start off dry, with 
conditions declining into the afternoon and evening. There 
remains a bit of spread among the deterministic models, though 
the AI GFS and ECMWF are in fairly good agreement that there 
will be unsettled conditions as an 850 mb open wave tries to 
close off across western NY. This would lead to increasing 
southwest flow and higher PWATs advecting into the region, with 
values around 1.5 inches.

It's worth mentioning there is strong 1030+ mb high pressure 
building to the north during this time, and depending on the 
setup, this could suppress Sunday's system farther south. Yet 
another thing to monitor. Beyond Sunday into early next week, 
there is variability in the forecast, mainly with the arrival of
high pressure expanding out of Quebec. This may impact how 
quickly the moisture departs Sunday into Monday.
